summary: Specifies RIPng, a routing protocol for IPv6 internets, based on the algorithms already widely used by RIP in IPv4. It is a simple distance-vector protocol for smaller networks.

eli5.summary: Neighbors tell each other how far away places are, so each knows which way to go. RIPng is that for the new internet addresses.

questions: what is the ripng multicast address
subtitle: RIP carried over to IPv6: the same simple distance-vector routing, with 128-bit prefixes in each route entry.

tldr.problem: IPv6 networks needed an interior routing protocol, and the widely used IPv4 protocol RIP could not carry 128-bit IPv6 prefixes.
tldr.mechanism: RIPng keeps RIP's distance-vector algorithm, 30-second updates and metric limit of 15, but sends 20-byte route table entries over UDP port 521 to the multicast group FF02::9.
tldr.outcome: RIPng is a Proposed Standard with the same limits as RIP: it suits moderate-size networks, has a diameter of at most 15 hops and uses fixed metrics.

today: RFC 2080 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC itself describes version 1 of the protocol.

sections.title: Why RIPng Exists
sections.content:
RIPng is a routing protocol for an IPv6 internet. The RFC calls it the minimum change to the Routing Information Protocol (RIP), as specified in RFC 1058 and RFC 1723, that is needed to work over IPv6.

It is a distance vector protocol (also called Bellman-Ford). It was designed as an Interior Gateway Protocol, meaning a protocol used inside one Autonomous System, and for moderate-size autonomous systems only. It is not meant for more complex environments.

The RFC lists three limits. The longest path, the network diameter, is 15 hops, assuming a cost of 1 per network. The protocol relies on counting to infinity to resolve some unusual situations, which can be slow or costly in a large looped network. And it uses fixed metrics, so it is not suited to choosing routes by measured delay, reliability or load.
sections.eli5: RIPng is a simple way for routers to share road maps with their neighbors. It works well in a small town, but it is not meant for a giant country.

sections.title: Routing Table, Metrics and Timers
sections.content:
Each router has a routing table with an entry for every reachable destination. An entry holds the IPv6 prefix, a metric (the total cost to reach it), the next hop address, a route change flag and timers. A network's metric is an integer from 1 to 15, and 1 is usually used, which makes the metric a simple hop count. The value 16 means infinity: the destination is unreachable.

Every 30 seconds a router sends an unsolicited Response with its complete routing table to its neighbors. To stop routers from synchronizing their updates, implementations must either use a clock not affected by system load or add a random offset of up to 15 seconds in either direction to the timer.

Each route has two timers. If 180 seconds pass without an update for a route, it times out. Its metric is set to 16, the garbage-collection timer is set for 120 seconds, and the route stays in updates until that timer expires so neighbors learn it is gone. A new route for the same network found in the meantime replaces it.
sections.eli5: Every router keeps a list of places and how many steps away they are. Every half minute it shares the list, and if a neighbor goes quiet for three minutes, the router decides those places cannot be reached any more.

sections.title: The RIPng Message Format
sections.content:
RIPng runs over UDP. Each router listens on UDP port 521, the RIPng port. Unsolicited updates use port 521 as both source and destination. Replies to a request go to the port the request came from, and specific queries may come from another port but must be sent to port 521 on the target.

A message has a 4-byte header with a command, a version (this document describes version 1) and two bytes that must be zero. After that comes a list of 20-byte route table entries (RTEs). Two commands exist: 1 is a request for all or part of the routing table, and 2 is a response carrying all or part of the sender's table.

An ordinary RTE holds a 16-byte IPv6 prefix, a 2-byte route tag, a 1-byte prefix length (0 to 128) and a 1-byte metric (1 to 15, or 16 for infinity). The route tag must be preserved and readvertised; its intended use is to separate internal RIPng routes from external ones imported from another protocol. The number of RTEs per message depends on the medium's MTU.
sections.eli5: Each message is a letter with a short header and then a list of lines. Every line says a place, how long its address is and how far away it is.

sections.title: Next Hop and Default Routes
sections.content:
RIP-2 puts a next hop in every entry. In RIPng that would nearly double the RTE size, so the next hop is given by a special RTE. It is marked by 0xFF in the metric field, and its prefix field holds the next hop IPv6 address. It applies to all following RTEs until the message ends or another next hop RTE appears. Its route tag and prefix length must be zero when sent and are ignored on receipt.

A next hop of 0:0:0:0:0:0:0:0 means the next hop is the router that sent the advertisement. A next hop address must be link-local; if it is not, it is treated as all zeros. The next hop RTE is advisory: ignoring it may give a sub-optimal but still valid route.

A prefix with length zero designates a default route. The RFC suggests using the prefix 0:0:0:0:0:0:0:0 for it. Default routes are handled like any other prefix, but they should generally not leave the boundary of an AS.
sections.eli5: Sometimes the best way to a place is through a different neighbor than the one telling you. A special line in the message says, go through that neighbor instead.

sections.title: Processing Requests, Responses and Updates
sections.content:
A router that has just started multicasts a Request for the whole table. A request with exactly one entry, with prefix zero, prefix length zero and metric 16, means send the entire table. Other requests are answered by looking up each entry and filling in its metric, or 16 if no route exists. Whole-table replies get normal Split Horizon processing; specific lookups do not, since they are expected to be for diagnostics.

A Response must come from the RIPng port and from a link-local source address, and must not be the router's own output. Multicast responses must also arrive with a hop count of 255, which proves the sender is a neighbor. Each RTE is validated: the prefix must not be multicast or link-local, the prefix length must be 0 to 128 and the metric 1 to 16. The router then computes metric = MIN (metric + cost, infinity).

A new route is added unless its metric is infinity. An existing route is replaced if the update comes from the same router with a different metric, or has a lower metric. Updates are sent to the multicast group FF02::9, the all-rip-routers group. When a metric changes, a triggered update is sent after a random delay of 1 to 5 seconds and need include only changed routes.
sections.eli5: When a router hears news from a neighbor, it adds the cost of the road to that neighbor and keeps the cheaper way. If something changes, it spreads the news quickly, but waits a few seconds so it does not shout too much.

sections.title: Split Horizon and Poisoned Reverse
sections.content:
Split Horizon avoids problems caused by sending a route back to the neighbor it was learned from. The basic form omits routes learned from a neighbor in updates sent to that neighbor. Split Horizon with Poisoned Reverse instead includes those routes but with metric 16, advertising that they are unreachable. The RFC calls this the preferred method.

Implementations should offer a per-interface setting to select no horizoning, split horizoning or poisoned reverse. Split Horizon is applied to triggered updates as well as regular ones.

Routes to link-local addresses must never be included in an RTE, and routes with infinite metrics must still be included in updates.
sections.eli5: If a friend told you the way to the park, you do not tell them the way back to the park. With poisoned reverse you do say it, but you add, you cannot get there through me.

sections.title: Controls and Security
sections.content:
Section 3 describes optional administrative controls. They are not part of the protocol, but the RFC strongly recommends including some. Examples are a neighbor list, so a router accepts responses only from listed neighbors, and filters that allow or disallow specific destination prefixes on an interface, in or out. By default no restrictions or filters apply.

For security, the RFC says only that RIPng runs over IPv6 and relies on the IP Authentication Header and the IP Encapsulating Security Payload for integrity and authentication or confidentiality of routing exchanges.
sections.eli5: A router can be told to listen only to neighbors it trusts, and the safety locks come from the internet layer underneath.
